question: Why do the Transformer authors scale the dot products by 1/sqrt(dk)?
answer:
The authors scale dot products by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ to counteract the effect of large values of $d_k$ [Attention Is All You Need, p.4]. For large $d_k$, dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions with extremely small gradients [Attention Is All You Need, p.4]. This scaling prevents the softmax from entering these problematic regions [Attention Is All You Need, p.4]. The dot products grow because, assuming query and key components are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has a variance of $d_k$ [Attention Is All You Need, p.4].

question: What BLEU score did the big Transformer reach on WMT 2014 English-to-German?
answer:
The big Transformer model achieved a BLEU score of 28.4 on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task [Attention Is All You Need, p.8]. This result established a new state-of-the-art, outperforming the best previously reported models, including ensembles, by more than 2.0 BLEU [Attention Is All You Need, p.8]. The paper also notes that this model was trained for 300,000 steps, which took 3.5 days on eight GPUs [Attention Is All You Need, p.7].

question: What are Moshi's theoretical and practical latencies?
answer:
Moshi has a theoretical latency of 160ms [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, p.26][Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, p.1][Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, p.41]. In practice, the latency is 200ms [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, p.1]. This performance is achieved by pretraining with an acoustic delay of 2 and finetuning with an acoustic delay of 1 [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, p.26].

question: What frame rate and bitrate does Moshi's neural audio codec use?
answer:
Moshi's neural audio codec, Mimi, operates at a frame rate of 12.5Hz and a bitrate of 1.1kbps [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, p.23]. This configuration is achieved using Q = 8 quantizers, each with a codebook size of NA = 2048 [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, p.11]. The codec is fully causal, which is crucial for achieving low latency in real-time dialogue [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, p.24].

answer:

question: What are the two components of the dynamic chunking mechanism in H-Net?
answer:
Based on the provided passages, the dynamic chunking mechanism in H-Net consists of two key components:

1.  **Chunking Layer**: This includes a routing module for dynamically drawing chunk boundaries and a downsampler that selectively retains vectors based on boundary indicators to reduce sequence length [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, p.3].
2.  **Dechunking Layer**: This includes a smoothing module for converting discrete chunks into interpolated representations and an upsampler that restores compressed vectors to their original resolution based on boundary indicators [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, p.3].

These components work together to compress data to a resolution similar to BPE tokenizers without external supervision [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, p.3].

question: By what factor does H-Net improve data efficiency on DNA modelling compared with isotropic models?
answer:
H-Net improves data efficiency on DNA modeling by a factor of 3.6 compared to isotropic models [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, p.4]. This means H-Net models achieve similar performance to isotropic models using approximately 3.6× less data [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, p.17]. Specifically, H-Net (1-stage) with an M3T1 encoder achieves 3.6× the data efficiency of an isotropic architecture [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, p.37].
